newsitem.title: LEBANON: Markets gain confidence in Lebanon - HSBC chief.
newsitem.headline: Markets gain confidence in Lebanon - HSBC chief.

text.p: International financial markets believe Lebanon is well managed under Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri and are gaining confidence in the country, a top international banker said.
Sir William Purves, chairman of HSBC Group plc, told a news conference in Beirut he expected the increased confidence to be reflected in the markets' response to Lebanon's next Eurobond issue.

"Things are being well managed and this brings confidence to international markets, and when the next large bond issue comes I think it will be well supported at lower margins than previous issues," Purves said.

He was speaking on Thursday evening after meeting Hariri, acting finance minister Fouad Siniora and Bank of Lebanon Governor Riad Salameh during a visit to Beirut marking 50 years in Lebanon of The British Bank of the Middle East, an HSBC group member.

"Prime Minister Hariri seems to me to have provided tremendous leadership in the last three years. Because of your prime minister and his team so much progress has actually been made (in Lebanon)," Purves said.
"I think internationally now there is much greater support for investment in Lebanon and we are seeing capital markets especially being developed," he added.
Purves said Hariri told him of his plans to reduce interest rates and increase investment in Lebanon next year after the new government currently under discussion is formed.
"The government dearly wants to see interest rates coming down," Purves said.

Rates of up to 22 percent on treasury bills combined with a steadily appreciating currency are attracting the cash the government needs to finance its huge budget deficit and service its mounting public debt, but some bankers and economists say they are also crowding out the private sector and hindering the economic growth Lebanon needs.
Asked about his discussions with the Lebanese leaders, Purves said Hariri told him of plans to develop the Lebanese capital markets that would help bring down interest rates.
"I think once this (new) government settles down I wouldn't be surprised if you saw some considerable progress and developments in capital markets after Christmas and in 1997," he said.

"The developments I would expect to see, I think will be structured in such a way so that local (interest) rates will come more into line with international rates," he added in response to a question.
HSBC, whose treasury department is the biggest in London, had been suggesting innovative ways to help Lebanon. "We're committed to help, so what I can say is watch this space," Purves said.
